artworks.title: The Shaker Office (1794)
artworks.galleryName: Shaker Gallery: the 1794 Shaker Office, moved from the Harvard Shaker Village in 1920 (steps; not wheelchair-accessible)
artworks.description: The office of the Shaker community in Harvard, built in 1794, where the Shakers met the outside world. Clara Endicott Sears had it moved to Fruitlands in 1920 and opened it in 1922 as the first Shaker museum in the United States, with one of the earliest collections of Shaker objects.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Daderot, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: The Seasonal Gallery building (1928)
artworks.galleryName: Seasonal Gallery (built in 1928 as the Native American Museum): Shaker exhibitions
artworks.description: Opened in 1928 as the Native American Museum, renamed the Seasonal Gallery in 2024. In 2026 it shows Shaker objects and a contemporary art installation in changing exhibitions.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Daderot, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: Fruitlands Farmhouse
artworks.galleryName: Fruitlands Farmhouse (1820s), home of the Alcotts’ 1843 Transcendentalist community (steps; not wheelchair-accessible)
artworks.description: The only building original to the site. Amos Bronson Alcott and Charles Lane began their Transcendentalist community here in 1843; ten-year-old Louisa May Alcott lived here and later wrote about it. It lasted seven months. Clara Endicott Sears restored the house and opened it as a museum in 1914.
artworks.imageCredit: Photo: Daderot, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
